title: Using Modules (Advanced)
description: Advanced: use ready-made tools from Python's standard library: math, random and datetime.

subLevels.title: Importing modules
subLevels.summary: Load a module with import and use the math module.

blocks.text: A module is a file of ready-made Python code. Python comes with many of them, called the standard library. import loads a module so you can use its tools with a dot.

explanation: import math loads the math module. Put imports at the top of your program.
math.sqrt() is the square root function inside math.
math.pi is a value stored in the module.

items: math: square roots, rounding up and down, pi.
datetime: dates and days between them.

blocks.code:
import math
print(math.floor(4.7))
print(math.ceil(4.2))
books = 23
per_box = 5
print(math.ceil(books / per_box), "boxes")
explanation: floor() rounds down to a whole number; ceil() rounds up.
23 / 5 is 4.6; you need 5 boxes, so ceil() is the right tool.

blocks.text: from math import sqrt, pi brings in only the names you list, and you use them without math. in front.

blocks.code:
from math import sqrt, pi
print(sqrt(81))
print(f"{pi:.2f}")

blocks.text: import math as m loads math but lets you call it by a shorter name.

items: from math import sqrt: use sqrt(9).
import math as m: use m.sqrt(9).

blocks.caption: Only the last line of the error is shown.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Mixing the styles. After import math you must write math.sqrt(16); plain sqrt only works after from math import sqrt.

On a computer you can install extra modules with a tool called pip, and you can write your own module file, like helpers.py, and import it. The PyPath app works offline and runs a single main.py, so neither is possible in the Practical tab. This course only uses modules that come with Python.

blocks.title: In the app
blocks.text: The Practical tab includes standard library modules such as math, random and datetime. A few modules, like the ones for the internet, are blocked.
import gives you ready-made, tested tools, so you don't have to write them yourself.

questions.explanation: math.sqrt() gives the square root as a float, so the square root of 49 prints as 7.0.
questions.hint: Recall the kind of number math.sqrt(25) printed in the lesson.
optionFeedback: The answer is 7, but sqrt() returns a float, so it shows a decimal point.
sqrt() finds the square root; it doesn't print the number you gave it.
Right: sqrt() always gives a float.
math is imported and math.sqrt is written in full, so every name is known.

options: math has to be imported twice
After import math, sqrt must be written as math.sqrt
sqrt() only works on even numbers
questions.explanation: import math makes the name math available. sqrt on its own is unknown: NameError.
questions.hint: Think about which name import math actually makes available to your program.
optionFeedback: One import is enough; the problem is how sqrt is written.
Right: use math.sqrt, or change the import to from math import sqrt.
sqrt() works on any positive number, odd or even.
Imports go at the top, before you use the module.

questions.explanation: from math import ceil brings ceil in directly, so it can be used without math. in front.
questions.hint: The line names the module first, then the single tool you want to bring in.
optionFeedback: Right: from math import ceil.
import math import ceil is not valid Python; the first word is different.
Python has no use keyword for modules.
Python has no get keyword for modules.

questions.explanation: floor() rounds 7.9 down to 7; ceil() rounds 7.1 up to 8.
questions.hint: One of these functions always rounds down and the other always rounds up.
optionFeedback: That would be normal rounding; floor() always goes down and ceil() always goes up.
ceil() rounds up, so 7.1 becomes 8.
floor() rounds down, so 7.9 becomes 7.
Right: floor goes down, ceil goes up.

questions.prompt: What does import math as m do?
options: Imports math and lets you call it m, as in m.sqrt(4)
Imports only a function called m
Renames the math module file on your phone
Multiplies every math result by m
questions.explanation: as gives the module a nickname inside your program. The real module is unchanged.
questions.hint: Compare it with plain import math and think about what the extra part changes.
optionFeedback: Right: m becomes a short name for math.
It imports the whole math module; m is just its new name.
Nothing on your phone changes; the nickname only exists while your program runs.
as only gives a name; it doesn't do any maths.

subLevels.title: random and datetime
subLevels.summary: Make random choices and work with dates.

blocks.code:
import random
dice = random.randint(1, 6)
print("You rolled", dice)
snacks = ["samosa", "idli", "poha"]
print(random.choice(snacks))
random.shuffle(snacks)
print(snacks)
explanation: randint(1, 6) gives a whole number from 1 to 6. Unlike range(), both ends are included.
choice() picks one item from a list.
shuffle() mixes up the list itself.
blocks.caption: Run it a few times: the results change.

blocks.code:
import random
cards = [1, 2, 3]
cards = random.shuffle(cards)
print(cards)

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Writing cards = random.shuffle(cards). Like sort(), shuffle() changes the list and returns None, so the list is lost. Just write random.shuffle(cards).

pages.title: The same random numbers every time

blocks.text: random.seed() picks the starting point of the random numbers. With the same seed you get the same numbers every run, which is handy for testing a game.
Without a seed the numbers change every run; with the same seed they repeat exactly.
The datetime module has a date type. date(year, month, day) makes a date.

blocks.code:
from datetime import date
exam = date(2026, 3, 15)
print(exam)
print(exam.year, exam.month, exam.day)

blocks.caption: Shows today's date, so the output depends on the day you run it.

blocks.code:
from datetime import date, timedelta
start = date(2026, 1, 28)
print(start + timedelta(days=7))
holiday = date(2026, 3, 4)
gap = holiday - start
print(gap.days, "days to go")
explanation: timedelta(days=7) is a length of time; adding it moves the date on, into February.
Subtracting two dates gives a timedelta; .days is the number of days.

items: random.randint(a, b): a whole number from a to b.

questions.explanation: randint() includes both ends, so 1, 2 and 3 are all possible.
questions.hint: Remember how randint() treats its second number compared with range().
optionFeedback: That is how range(1, 3) works; randint() includes the end number too.
randint(1, 3) starts at 1, not 0.
Right: both ends are included.
randint() only gives whole numbers.

options: shuffle() changes the list itself and returns None
Lists of letters can't be shuffled
questions.explanation: shuffle() works like sort(): it changes the list and gives back None, which is then stored in deck.
questions.code:
import random
deck = ["A", "K", "Q"]
deck = random.shuffle(deck)
print(deck)
questions.hint: Think about what shuffle() gives back, and what deck = then stores.
optionFeedback: Right: deck = stores the None that shuffle() returns.
shuffle() keeps every item; it only changes their order.
Any list can be shuffled, whatever is inside it.
One import is enough to use random.shuffle().

questions.explanation: Both numbers come right after random.seed(5), so they are the same number: a == b is True.
questions.code:
import random
random.seed(5)
a = random.randint(1, 1000)
random.seed(5)
b = random.randint(1, 1000)
print(a == b)
questions.hint: Notice that the same seed is set again before the second number is made.
optionFeedback: Setting the same seed again restarts the same sequence, so a and b match.
Right: the same seed gives the same number.
A seed makes the numbers repeat exactly, on every run.
Comparing two numbers with == is always allowed.

questions.explanation: choice() picks one item from the list. With only one item, it must pick red.
questions.hint: Count how many items the list has to choose from.
optionFeedback: choice() returns one item, not the whole list.
choice() picks an item from the list, not a letter from the item.
choice() returns the item itself, not its position.
Right: the only item in the list is picked.

questions.explanation: date(2026, 12, 25) is year 2026, month 12, day 25, so .month is 12.
questions.code:
from datetime import date
d = date(2026, 12, 25)
print(d.month)
questions.hint: date() takes its three numbers in the order year, month, day.
optionFeedback: 25 is the day; the month is the middle number.
Right: the month is the second number.
That is what print(d) shows; .month gives just one part.
.month is a number, not the month's name.

questions.explanation: January has 31 days, so 3 days after 30 January is 2 February.
questions.code:
from datetime import date, timedelta
d = date(2026, 1, 30)
print(d + timedelta(days=3))
questions.hint: Count forward one day at a time and remember how many days January has.
optionFeedback: Right: 31 January, 1 February, 2 February.
Dates move into the next month; there is no 33 January.
Count again: January has 31 days, so it is one day earlier than that.
Adding days moves the date forward, it doesn't change the month back.

questions.explanation: From 1 May to 10 May is 9 days, so gap.days is 9.
questions.code:
from datetime import date
gap = date(2026, 5, 10) - date(2026, 5, 1)
print(gap.days)
questions.hint: Subtract the day numbers, because both dates are in the same month.
optionFeedback: Subtracting dates gives the gap between them, not the number of dates counted.
Check the subtraction again: 10 - 1.
Right: 10 - 1 is 9 days.
The later date comes first, so the gap is positive.

cheatSheet.title: Using Modules

items.note: Use the module name and a dot.
Give the module a short name.
A whole number from 1 to 6, both included.
Pick one item from a list.
The same seed gives the same numbers.

items.code:
from datetime import date, timedelta
d = date(2026, 1, 30)
print(d + timedelta(days=3))
items.note: Make dates and move them on.

items.code:
from datetime import date
print((date(2026, 5, 10) - date(2026, 5, 1)).days)

remember: Imports go at the top of the program.
The app has Python's standard library only: no pip and no module files of your own.
